cls: Immunomodulator - humanized anti-CD25 (IL-2 receptor alpha) monoclonal antibody (WITHDRAWN from market 2018)
pharm: Humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds CD25 (the alpha subunit of the high-affinity interleukin-2 receptor), modulating IL-2 signaling and expanding immunoregulatory CD56-bright natural killer cells; the multiple sclerosis product (Zinbryta) was withdrawn worldwide in March 2018 due to serious immune-mediated brain and liver injury.
tags: Anti-CD25 / IL-2 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody

Subcutaneous injection; not related to meals
Limited human data; discontinued and not used - monoclonal antibodies cross the placenta in later pregnancy
Unknown if excreted in human milk; product withdrawn - not used
No specific dose adjustment described (monoclonal antibody, not renally cleared)
CONTRAINDICATED in pre-existing hepatic disease/impairment and autoimmune hepatitis (boxed hepatotoxicity warning)
Avoid - additive hepatotoxicity risk given boxed warning for severe liver injury
Monthly transaminases (ALT/AST) and bilirubin before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose
summary: Daclizumab (Zinbryta) was a humanized anti-CD25 (IL-2 receptor alpha) monoclonal antibody dosed at 150 mg subcutaneously once monthly for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis. IMPORTANT: It was WITHDRAWN from the market worldwide in March 2018 after reports of serious inflammatory brain disorders (encephalitis and meningoencephalitis) and severe autoimmune hepatotoxicity, and it is NOT currently available - this record is provided for reference and historical completeness only. While marketed it carried a BOXED WARNING for hepatic injury (including autoimmune hepatitis and fatal liver failure) and for immune-mediated disorders (skin reactions, lymphadenopathy, and noninfectious colitis). Because of these risks its use was restricted under a REMS to patients who had an inadequate response to two or more other multiple sclerosis therapies. An older daclizumab formulation (Zenapax), used for prophylaxis of transplant rejection, was also discontinued. Do not present daclizumab as a current treatment option.
indications: WITHDRAWN (2018) - listed for historical reference only; not currently available for any indication
While marketed (Zinbryta): relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis in adults
Use was RESTRICTED to patients who had an inadequate response to two or more other drugs indicated for the treatment of multiple sclerosis, owing to the safety profile
Historical (Zenapax, separate older formulation, also discontinued): prophylaxis of acute organ rejection in renal transplant recipients as part of an immunosuppressive regimen

dosage.n: PRODUCT WITHDRAWN 2018 - not available; dose shown for historical reference only

dosage.d: 150 mg once monthly was the only labeled dose; a missed dose was given as soon as possible if within 2 weeks, then resuming the usual monthly schedule

admin: Administered by subcutaneous injection (Zinbryta prefilled syringe/autoinjector) into the thigh, abdomen, or back of the upper arm; rotate injection sites
Obtain baseline serum transaminases and total bilirubin before initiating, and monthly LFTs before each dose while on therapy
Bring the prefilled syringe to room temperature before injecting; do not shake; inspect for particulates
While marketed, dispensed only through a restricted distribution program (REMS) because of the risk of hepatotoxicity and immune-mediated disorders
NOTE: The product was withdrawn from the market worldwide in March 2018 and is no longer manufactured or distributed - administration details are historical
moa: Daclizumab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds to CD25 (Tac/IL-2R-alpha), the alpha subunit of the high-affinity interleukin-2 (IL-2) receptor expressed on activated T lymphocytes. By blocking CD25, it modulates IL-2 signaling: it reduces the high-affinity IL-2-driven activation and expansion of effector/activated T cells while redirecting IL-2 to intermediate-affinity receptors, leading to expansion of immunoregulatory CD56-bright natural killer (NK) cells that can selectively limit activated T cells. The net immunomodulatory effect was thought to reduce the inflammatory activity underlying relapsing multiple sclerosis. The precise mechanism by which it exerted therapeutic effects in MS was not fully established.

absolute: Pre-existing hepatic disease or hepatic impairment, including serum transaminases at least 2 times the upper limit of normal
History of serious hypersensitivity reaction to daclizumab or any excipient
relative: Concomitant use of other hepatotoxic drugs or other immunosuppressants/disease-modifying MS therapies
Active or chronic infection (immunomodulation increases infection risk)
Pre-existing autoimmune conditions or history of severe skin reactions
monitor: Serum transaminases (ALT, AST) and total bilirubin monthly before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose
Signs and symptoms of hepatic injury, immune-mediated disorders, infection, and depression/suicidal ideation
Skin for new or worsening rash and lymph nodes for lymphadenopathy

preg: There were limited human data. As an IgG monoclonal antibody, daclizumab could cross the placenta, especially in the second and third trimesters. While marketed, use in pregnancy was advised only if the potential benefit justified the potential risk to the fetus, and effective contraception was recommended during and for some months after therapy. The product is now WITHDRAWN and is not used.
lact: It is not known whether daclizumab was excreted in human milk; human immunoglobulin G is present in milk. While marketed, the decision to discontinue nursing or the drug was to weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against the maternal need for therapy. The product is now WITHDRAWN and is not used.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment was described for renal impairment; as a monoclonal antibody, daclizumab is degraded by catabolism rather than renal elimination.
hepatic: CONTRAINDICATED in patients with pre-existing hepatic disease or hepatic impairment (including transaminases at least 2x ULN) and in those with autoimmune hepatitis. Daclizumab carried a BOXED WARNING for hepatic injury including autoimmune hepatitis and fatal/serious liver failure; transaminases and bilirubin were monitored monthly before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose, with prompt discontinuation for significant elevations or clinical hepatic injury. The product has since been WITHDRAWN from the market.

major: Other hepatotoxic drugs (including other agents associated with liver injury) - additive risk of severe hepatic injury given the boxed hepatotoxicity warning
Live attenuated vaccines - avoid during immunomodulatory therapy (risk of vaccine-related infection)
Other immunosuppressants or disease-modifying MS therapies - additive immunosuppression/infection risk
moderate: CYP450-metabolized drugs - chronic inflammation suppresses certain CYP enzymes; reducing inflammation could alter their metabolism (clinical significance uncertain)
Concomitant immunomodulators or biologics - additive immune effects
minor: No significant small-molecule pharmacokinetic interactions were established for this monoclonal antibody
interactions.food: Not applicable (subcutaneous injection); not affected by food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol due to additive risk of hepatotoxicity given the boxed warning for severe liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Obtain baseline and monthly serum transaminases and total bilirubin; assess hepatitis serologies and screen for infection before initiation per labeling while marketed.

common: Nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections
serious: Hepatotoxicity including autoimmune hepatitis and liver failure (BOXED WARNING)
Immune-mediated encephalitis and meningoencephalitis (a key reason for market withdrawal)
Hemolytic anemia and other immune-mediated disorders
rare: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)-type or other severe cutaneous reactions
emergency: Acute or fulminant liver failure (jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy)
Encephalitis or meningoencephalitis (altered mental status, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, fever, headache)

monitoring: Serum transaminases (ALT, AST) and total bilirubin monthly before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose (BOXED WARNING - hepatotoxicity)
Signs and symptoms of hepatic injury (jaundice, dark urine, right upper quadrant pain, fatigue, anorexia)
Neurologic status for encephalitis/meningoencephalitis (altered mental status, seizures, fever, headache)
New or worsening skin rash and lymphadenopathy; gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting noninfectious colitis
Signs of infection and depression/suicidal ideation
counsel: This product (Zinbryta) was WITHDRAWN from the market in 2018 because of serious brain inflammation and liver injury - it is no longer available and should not be used; this information is for reference only

While it was in use, monthly blood tests for liver function were required before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose; patients were told to report yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, nausea, or right-sided abdominal pain immediately
Patients were warned to report fever, severe headache, confusion, seizures, or other new neurologic symptoms (possible encephalitis) without delay
Report any new or worsening rash, swollen glands, or persistent diarrhea/abdominal pain (possible immune-mediated colitis)
Avoid alcohol and other liver-toxic drugs; do not receive live vaccines while on immunomodulatory therapy
pk: Gradual immunomodulatory effect over weeks; CD56-bright NK cell expansion within weeks of dosing
Subcutaneous peak (Tmax) approximately 5-7 days after a dose
Supports once-monthly subcutaneous dosing; pharmacodynamic effects persist after discontinuation
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze; protect from light; allow to reach room temperature before injection (historical labeling)
pearls: WITHDRAWN 2018: Daclizumab (Zinbryta) was voluntarily withdrawn from the market worldwide in March 2018 after cases of serious immune-mediated encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and severe autoimmune hepatitis - it is NOT available and is included here for historical/reference completeness only

BOXED WARNING (while marketed): hepatic injury including autoimmune hepatitis and fatal liver failure - contraindicated in pre-existing hepatic disease/impairment and autoimmune hepatitis; required monthly transaminase and bilirubin monitoring before each dose and for 6 months after the last dose
BOXED WARNING (while marketed): other immune-mediated disorders including severe skin reactions, lymphadenopathy, and noninfectious colitis
Mechanism: binds CD25 (IL-2 receptor alpha), modulates IL-2 signaling, and expands immunoregulatory CD56-bright NK cells; dose was 150 mg subcutaneously once monthly
Because of its safety profile, use was restricted (via a REMS) to patients with inadequate response to two or more other MS disease-modifying therapies; do not present it as a current option
A separate older daclizumab product (Zenapax) used for transplant rejection prophylaxis was also discontinued
missed: Not applicable in current practice - the product is WITHDRAWN and no longer available. Historically (while marketed), if a once-monthly dose was missed it was administered as soon as possible (if within about 2 weeks of the scheduled date), after which the usual monthly schedule resumed; doses were not doubled.
overdose: No specific overdose data or antidote were established. Management would be supportive with close monitoring, particularly of hepatic function (transaminases, bilirubin) given the boxed hepatotoxicity warning, and for neurologic and immune-mediated effects. The product is WITHDRAWN and no longer in clinical use.
